scoringInsight: Check the arithmetic before allocating effort. Relevant experience (1.2, 20 points), services in the last three years with samples (2.2, 15) and geographical reach (2.4, 10) are 45 points on their own; add qualifications of key staff (3.1, 15) and 60 of the 70 technical points are awarded on credentials, samples, footprint and named people rather than on argument. Understanding of the ToR (1.1, 5) and methodology (2.1, 5) together carry 10. So the part EY can write unaided, the framing and the work plan, is worth at most a seventh of the technical score, and a perfect five-page body cannot rescue a thin annex. Effort must therefore go where the points are: assignment sheets, cleared samples, CVs and a defensible country-by-country geography claim. Drafting is cheap here. Clearance, consent and CV collection are the critical path and must start in week one of the bid, not the last.

referenceSpec: Three references are mandatory, not advisory. RFP Part 3 requires descriptions of similar projects and at least three client references. Fewer than three is a completeness failure before it is a scoring one, so treat this as a gate item in the compliance matrix rather than a nice-to-have.

Each reference must carry, as a minimum: client organisation; referee full name; referee job title; direct email address; telephone with country code; the EY assignment being referenced, with year and contract value; EY's role on that assignment; and the referee's written consent to be contacted by Conservation International, with the date consent was given.

Choose the three for coverage of the scoring criteria, not for client prestige. Reference 1 should sit closest to business model, options or feasibility design, which is the evidence for criterion 1.2. Reference 2 should sit closest to African tourism, destination or protected-area work, which is the evidence for criterion 2.4 and for the weakest of the eight minimum skills. Reference 3 should be an NGO, donor or public-sector client who can speak to delivery inside a fixed fee and a fixed timetable, which reassures on criterion 2.1 and on the credibility of a US$40,000 cap.

The referee must be the person who actually received and used the work, not the account relationship partner. An evaluator who telephones and finds the referee cannot describe the deliverable does more damage than no call at all.

Warm every referee before submission: confirm they still hold the role, that the email and number are current, that they will be reachable during CI's evaluation window, and that they know in one sentence what EY delivered. Record the date of that conversation next to the consent date.

Where a client cannot be named, agree the anonymised form in advance, for example 'a Southern African national tourism authority', and still supply a contactable referee. An anonymous assignment with no reachable referee scores nothing and invites the evaluator to discount the whole annex.

pastAssignmentSpec: Three different time windows are being tested and one undated list satisfies none of them. RFP Part 1 asks for relevant services undertaken in the past five years. Criterion 2.2 asks for relevant services provided in the last three years, with samples of work delivered. Criterion 1.2 asks for relevant experience of five to ten years. Build a single Annex C table with an explicit year column and tag each row with the criterion it serves, so the evaluator can see all three tests met on the face of the annex without doing arithmetic.

Target six to eight assignments. At least three must have completed within the last three years and each of those three must have a releasable sample attached, because criterion 2.2 is worth 15 points and is scored on the samples rather than on the descriptions. At least five must fall within the last five years. At least one must demonstrate that the practice's relevant work reaches back five to ten years, which is what criterion 1.2 is actually testing.

Fields required for every entry: client name or the agreed anonymised description; country or countries of delivery; start and end dates by month and year; contract value in USD; the EY legal entity that delivered it; EY's role; scope in three to four lines; the deliverables actually produced; and the measurable outcome or decision taken.

Every entry needs a one-line 'why this is relevant to CI'. Evaluators score relevance, not volume, and an impressive but unrelated assignment dilutes the annex rather than strengthening it. If the relevance line cannot be written honestly, drop the entry.

Prefer assignments whose shape matches this one: desk-based options or feasibility studies, business model or operating model design, revenue and funding-model design, multi-stakeholder or cross-border studies, and tourism, destination or conservation work in Africa. Two well-matched assignments outscore five large mismatched ones.

Mark clearly which entries belong to a consortium partner or subcontractor rather than to EY, naming the firm. Presenting a partner's track record as EY's own is the fastest way to lose an evaluator's trust in the whole annex.

Repeat for each of six to eight assignments. Supplied by the EY bid team.]]

Supplied by the EY bid team.]]

workSampleNote: Criterion 2.2 is worth 15 points and asks for relevant services provided in the last three years with samples of work delivered. Read strictly, it wants client work, which neither available item is. Handle them differently. The benchmark scan is the stronger asset by far and should be offered, but framed for what it is: EY's own pre-bid research on exactly this question, produced at EY's cost, covering 31 benchmarks across seven archetypes including both initiatives CI names. Offer a cleaned extract as an annex, not the working draft, and use it in the technical approach as the reason a 13-deep-dive programme fits inside 12 weeks and US$40,000. It is evidence of capability and of head start rather than of a client service, so do not file it under 2.2 as though it were an engagement; let it do its work in criteria 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 where it genuinely belongs. The instant payments point-of-view is a harder call and the honest assessment is that it is weak here. It is the right vintage and it does demonstrate transferable discipline: comparative analysis of delivery models across jurisdictions (UPI, Pix, PayShap), explicit scenario economics, and assumptions flagged rather than buried. But it is banking, not tourism or conservation, and a CI evaluator reading a payments deck in a protected-areas bid may reasonably infer that nothing closer exists. Recommendation: offer it only if two or three genuinely relevant client samples cannot be cleared in time. If it is offered, place it last in the annex, limit it to one or two representative pages rather than the full deck, and carry a single honest sentence saying it is included for method rather than subject. Both items need explicit release clearance, and the payments deck needs a confirmed external version, since a file marked v7 is an internal working version and may contain client-confidential material. The priority action for the bid team is not to polish these two; it is to find and clear two or three real client samples.
geographyArgument: Argue it in three layers and keep every layer falsifiable. First, network. EY member firms in the countries holding CI's priority areas, stated country by country with entity, office and consulting headcount. This is the claim a Big Four firm can make better than any boutique and it should lead. Second, delivery. Assignments actually run in Southern, Eastern and Western Africa in the last five years, named by country and year, because presence without delivery reads as a map rather than as experience. Third, subject familiarity. The evidence base for this assignment is itself Southern and Eastern African: a SADC-hosted secretariat, a Botswana-domiciled association, Kenyan and Namibian conservancy associations, a South African and Eswatini multi-agency pass. A Johannesburg-led team sits at the centre of gravity of that material, not at its edge, and that is a legitimate argument rather than a convenient one. Be honest about Western Africa. The published record is thin there for everyone working on this question, EY's is probably thinner, and francophone and lusophone reach needs named people rather than a network claim. Say so, and say it closes at inception once CI releases the list of 15.
